assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED transplanted cavity-QED physics to superconducting circuits, giving strong coupling, dispersive qubit readout and the architecture used across superconducting quantum processors and microwave quantum optics. It is original, clearly defined and has had broad, lasting impact on both fundamental quantum optics and quantum technology. I judge it with expertise in this area and acknowledge that this closeness may bias me in its favour.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 theory proposal (Blais et al.) and the first strong-coupling experiment (Wallraff, Schoelkopf and colleagues at Yale) are the decisive pair of contributions; the three proposed names cover theory and both experimental groups. Steven M. Girvin is a strong co-author of the theory and credit between him and Blais is not cleanly separable, so a three-person limit forces a contestable choice.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many independent groups over two decades; the interpretation is stable and the method is standard. It is close in subject to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits, which could be seen as either a natural follow-on or as too near that recognition.
uncertainties: Whether Girvin should replace Blais or Wallraff within the three-name limit.
Possible overlap in theme with the 2025 prize and whether the committee wants another superconducting-circuit award so soon.
My own field proximity means I may over-weight this entry.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 1995 Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions and its experimental realisation gave the first concrete, physically implementable scheme for a quantum computer. Trapped ions remain a leading platform with the highest gate fidelities, so the idea has clear originality and lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the evident theory originators; Rainer Blatt led key experimental demonstrations of gates, entanglement and algorithms in Innsbruck. The earlier 2012 prize for ion control and the experimental contribution of others (for example the NIST group) complicate fair credit, but I limit the proposal to the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Mature: gates and small algorithms have been demonstrated by many groups, and commercial devices exist. Timeliness is good given the 2025 prize on quantum circuit physics.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize and with candidates B045 and B027 that share Cirac and Zoller.
Whether the experimental credit should centre on Blatt or on groups outside the supplied list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction and fault-tolerant computation show that scalable quantum computation is possible in principle despite noise. Shor's code and Steane's codes, together with Kitaev's topological code and fault-tolerance ideas, are foundational and increasingly experimentally relevant, in line with the error-correction requirement I consider essential for useful processors.
assessment.attribution: Shor and Steane independently introduced the first quantum error-correcting codes; Kitaev introduced topological, fault-tolerant ideas. Others (Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme, Preskill, Aharonov, Ben-Or, Zurek) are not in the supplied names, so the credit is incomplete and arguably cannot be fairly cut to three.
assessment.maturity: The theory is mature, and recent experiments on below-threshold logical qubits strengthen the case, but demonstrations of full fault tolerance at scale are still in progress, so recognition could be slightly early or could be considered theory-heavy.
uncertainties: Credit is spread over many contributors beyond the supplied names.
Whether the experimental demonstration of the full scheme is considered sufficiently mature.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Loss and DiVincenzo's 1998 proposal and the subsequent demonstrations of single-spin readout, coherent control and two-qubit gates in quantum dots established semiconductor spin qubits, a platform compatible with industrial fabrication. The work is original and has clear impact on solid-state quantum information.
assessment.attribution: Loss is the theoretical originator, with David DiVincenzo as co-author who is not among the supplied names; Vandersypen and Marcus have major experimental roles, along with groups such as Tarucha and Kouwenhoven not listed. Attribution is therefore only partly supportable.
assessment.maturity: Experiments are well confirmed and fidelities in silicon are now high, but the platform is still developing relative to superconducting and ion systems.
uncertainties: Omitted contributors such as DiVincenzo, Tarucha and Kouwenhoven.
Overlap with B039, which carries a similar topic with different names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics and quantum acoustics demonstrated ground-state cooling, quantum control and entanglement of macroscopic mechanical objects, close in spirit to the macroscopic-quantum tests of the 2025 prize. The work is original and has relevance for sensing and quantum transduction.
assessment.attribution: Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg led optomechanics in optical systems; Cleland demonstrated quantum control of a mechanical resonator coupled to a superconducting qubit. Others (for example Painter, Lehnert, Harris) also made decisive contributions, so a three-person division is somewhat arbitrary.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed across several platforms, but the field is still evolving and applications beyond force sensing are developing, so it is moderately mature.
uncertainties: Several equally credible contributors are left out.
Whether the impact is broad enough relative to other quantum-technology candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84 and the Ekert entanglement-based protocol) is a conceptual foundation of quantum information science and led to practical secure communication, with deep links to Bell-inequality tests. Its originality and importance are clear.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard authored BB84; Ekert introduced the E91 entanglement-based protocol; all three names are supported. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is an acknowledged precedent that is not in the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: The idea dates from 1984 and 1991 and is well confirmed by experiments and deployed systems, so recognition is mature, though practical security claims remain debated.
uncertainties: Wiesner's precedent and whether it requires adjusting the credit.
Whether the committee considers it physics or primarily information science.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators and their experimental discovery in HgTe opened the field of topological phases protected by time-reversal symmetry. It is highly original, widely influential and conceptually clean, though outside my own research area.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the theoretical prediction; Molenkamp's group performed the HgTe experiment following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, Fu, and Moore and Balents are not listed, so credit is contested beyond the names supplied.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed across materials and techniques over nearly two decades; very mature and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: The credit of BHZ, Fu-Kane-Mele and Moore-Balents.
I am judging a condensed-matter topic outside my own specialty.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, including the superfluid to Mott-insulator transition and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopes, provides controllable many-body quantum systems and is influential across atomic, condensed-matter and quantum-information physics.
assessment.attribution: The supplied credit is large (five names) and spans theory (Cirac, Zoller, Dalibard) and experiment (Bloch, Greiner). The Jaksch et al. proposal and the Greiner/Bloch Mott transition are central, so a three-person prize needs a thematic slice and would omit others.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with many independent confirmations, though the long-term goal of useful analogue simulation remains partly unrealised. Its closeness to earlier cold-atom prizes (BEC, 2001) may count against it.
uncertainties: Strong overlap with B045, B015 and B017 in Cirac and Zoller.
Whether credit can be fairly restricted to three people.
